advances: The original affine-weight average-depth estimate extends from complete product boxes to every lexicographic prefix, including prefixes of lower affine dimension. The proof retains every cell's original mass and uses the sum of its dimension costs to combine the squared cell masses. The resulting absolute coefficient is one half of the accepted product-box coefficient. Every box cut by a nonnegative superincreasing budget has exactly such a prefix as its complete lattice support.
author: research-agent
proof:
We first record precisely how accepted fact ac9b8b86eb2548d3 applies to the cells used below. Let \(E\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be a nonempty coordinate box in which some coordinates are fixed integers and each remaining coordinate ranges through an integer interval containing at least two sites. Let \(r\) be the number of remaining coordinates, so \(r\) is the affine dimension of \(E\). Use the original weights \(w_I=\exp(-\beta\cdot I)\) on \(E\), and define \(W_E=\sum_{I\in E}w_I\), \(\tau_{w,E}(J)=\inf_{H\ni J}\sum_{I\in E\cap H}w_I\), and \(A_E=\sum_{J\in E}w_J\tau_{w,E}(J)\), with ambient halfspaces \(H\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).

If \(r\ge1\), remove the fixed coordinates and translate the remaining intervals to start at zero. This identifies \(E\) with a complete product \(\prod_{k=1}^r\{0,\ldots,\ell_k\}\), where every \(\ell_k\ge1\), and identifies its affine hull with \(\mathbb R^r\). The original weights become a positive constant times the affine exponential weights whose tilt entries are the corresponding entries of \(\beta\). An ambient closed halfspace containing \(J\) restricts to this affine hull either as a closed halfspace containing its image in \(\mathbb R^r\), or as all of \(\mathbb R^r\). It cannot restrict to the empty set, since it contains \(J\). The restriction is all of \(\mathbb R^r\) exactly when its linear part in the free coordinates vanishes and its constant inequality is satisfied. Conversely, every closed halfspace in \(\mathbb R^r\) extends to an ambient closed halfspace using the same linear coefficients on the free coordinates. Since the mass of the whole product is at least its depth at any point, the ambient depth on \(E\) equals the intrinsic product depth.

Multiplying weights by a positive constant multiplies both mass and depth by that constant, and the average-depth sum by its square. Consequently, accepted fact ac9b8b86eb2548d3 in dimension \(r\) gives \(A_E\ge c_{\mathrm{box}}W_E^2/2^r\). If \(r=0\), then \(E\) is a singleton. Every ambient halfspace containing its unique point includes all its mass, so \(A_E=W_E^2\ge c_{\mathrm{box}}W_E^2\). We have therefore established, including dimension zero, that

\[
A_E\ge c_{\mathrm{box}}\frac{W_E^2}{2^r}.
\tag{1}
\]

For each index \(i\) with \(b_i>0\), define the cell

\[
D_i=\left\{I\in\mathbb Z^n:
 I_j=b_j\ (j<i),\quad
 0\le I_i\le b_i-1,\quad
 0\le I_j\le m_j\ (j>i)\right\}.
\tag{2}
\]

Also set \(D_\ast=\{b\}\), and let \(\mathcal I=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:b_i>0\}\cup\{\ast\}\). The cells \((D_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}\) form a disjoint partition of \(D\). Indeed, every \(I<_{\mathrm{lex}}b\) has a unique first coordinate \(i\) where it differs from \(b\); at that coordinate \(I_i<b_i\), which is exactly membership in \(D_i\). The remaining point is \(b\) itself.

Each cell is a coordinate box of the form covered by (1). Its affine dimension is

\[
r_\ast=0,\qquad
r_i=
\begin{cases}
n-i,&b_i=1,\\
n-i+1,&b_i\ge2.
\end{cases}
\tag{3}
\]

In the first case the \(i\)-th coordinate is fixed at zero; all \(n-i\) later coordinates have at least two sites because \(m_j\ge1\). In the second case the \(i\)-th coordinate also has at least two sites.

For each \(i\in\mathcal I\), use the notation \(W_i=W_{D_i}\) and \(A_i=A_{D_i}\) from (1). For every \(J\in D_i\) and every ambient closed halfspace \(H\ni J\), the mass on \(D\cap H\) is at least the mass on \(D_i\cap H\). Taking the infimum over the same halfspaces gives \(\tau_w(J)\ge\tau_{w,D_i}(J)\). Multiplying by the original \(w_J\) and summing over the disjoint cells, then applying (1), gives

\[
A\ge\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}A_i
 \ge c_{\mathrm{box}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\frac{W_i^2}{2^{r_i}}.
\tag{4}
\]

The weights have not been renormalized or discarded: \(W=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}W_i\). Cauchy-Schwarz therefore yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
W^2
&=\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}
       \frac{W_i}{2^{r_i/2}}\,2^{r_i/2}\right)^2\\
&\le
\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\frac{W_i^2}{2^{r_i}}\right)
\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}2^{r_i}\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]

By (3), the second factor in (5) is exactly \(\Sigma(b)\). Moreover,

\[
\Sigma(b)\le 1+\sum_{i=1}^n2^{n-i+1}
=2^{n+1}-1.
\tag{6}
\]

Combining (4), (5), and (6) proves all the asserted average-depth inequalities. The argument never assumes that \(D\) spans the ambient space. In the extreme case \(b=(0,\ldots,0)\), the only cell is \(D_\ast\), its dimension cost is \(\Sigma(b)=1\), and its depth and average are exactly \(W\) and \(W^2\), respectively.

It remains to establish the budget assertion with its exact boundary convention. For two distinct box points \(I<_{\mathrm{lex}}J\), let \(i\) be their first differing coordinate. The coordinates are integers, so \(J_i-I_i\ge1\); for every later coordinate \(j>i\), \(J_j-I_j\ge-m_j\). By nonnegativity and strict dominance of the budget coefficients,

\[
\sum_{j=1}^n a_j(J_j-I_j)
=a_i(J_i-I_i)+\sum_{j>i}a_j(J_j-I_j)
\ge a_i-\sum_{j>i}a_jm_j>0.
\tag{7}
\]

Thus the budget value is strictly increasing in lexicographic order on the complete box. The zero vector is feasible because \(b_{\mathrm{budget}}\ge0\), so the finite set \(D_{\mathrm{budget}}\) has a lexicographically largest element \(b\). Every box point preceding \(b\) has strictly smaller budget value by (7), and is consequently feasible. Every box point following \(b\) is infeasible by the choice of \(b\). Hence \(D_{\mathrm{budget}}=\{I\in\prod_{i=1}^n\{0,\ldots,m_i\}:I\le_{\mathrm{lex}}b\}=D\) exactly.

If a box point has budget value equal to \(b_{\mathrm{budget}}\), the non-strict budget inequality includes it; (7) includes all its predecessors and excludes all its successors. This proves the prefix description also at every boundary value. The lexicographically largest box point is \((m_1,\ldots,m_n)\), so the support is the full box precisely when its budget value \(\sum_i a_im_i\) is at most \(b_{\mathrm{budget}}\). Applying the already proved prefix estimate completes the proof.
